steps.text: Find the acceleration of the blocks, in m/s².

items.description: mass of the uniform disc pulley
items.name: M

items: g is a uniform constant of the stated value.
The string is light and inextensible and does not slip on the pulley.
The pulley is a uniform solid disc turning without axle friction.

steps.text: Apply Newton's second law to each hanging block and the rotational form of the second law to the pulley, with the string not slipping. Combining them gives one equation of motion for the whole system, in which the pulley adds an effective mass.

steps.description: effective inertial mass of the system
steps.principle: Newton's second law for each block, the rotational law tau = I alpha with I = (1/2) M R^2 for the disc, and the no-slip condition a = alpha R
steps.why: The two tensions differ because the pulley has inertia: (T2 - T1) R = (1/2) M R^2 (a / R), so T2 - T1 = (M/2) a. Adding the block equations then shows that the whole system accelerates as if it had the inertial mass m1 + m2 + M/2.

steps.principle: Newton's second law for the system: net driving force = effective mass x acceleration
steps.why: The net force along the string is the difference of the weights, (m2 - m1) g, and it must accelerate the effective inertial mass; dividing gives the common acceleration of the blocks.

steps.text: Taking M to zero gives the ideal Atwood result (m2 - m1) g / (m1 + m2), and equal masses give zero acceleration. The acceleration is always smaller than g, and the units N / kg give m/s^2.
acceleration of the blocks: 2.178 m/s²

Step 3. Assumptions: g is a uniform constant of the stated value. The string is light and inextensible and does not slip on the pulley. The pulley is a uniform solid disc turning without axle friction.
Step 4. Approach: Apply Newton's second law to each hanging block and the rotational form of the second law to the pulley, with the string not slipping. Combining them gives one equation of motion for the whole system, in which the pulley adds an effective mass.
Step 5. Newton's second law for each block, the rotational law tau = I alpha with I = (1/2) M R^2 for the disc, and the no-slip condition a = alpha R. Step 8. Answer: acceleration of the blocks: 2.178 m/s².

steps.principle: Newton's second law for the tangential motion, m L theta'' = -m g sin(theta), with sin(theta) approximately theta for small angles, giving omega^2 = g / L and T = 2 pi sqrt(L / g)
steps.why: The string tension is perpendicular to the motion, so only the tangential weight component restores the bob; for a small angle this is linear in theta and the equation is that of a harmonic oscillator whose period depends only on L and g.

Step 2. Given: V = 12 V (battery emf; given); R1 = 6 Ω (first resistor; given); R2 = 12 Ω (second resistor; given)
Step 3. Assumptions: The battery has negligible internal resistance and the wires have negligible resistance. Both resistors are ohmic.

Step 5. Approach: Each resistor of a parallel pair has the full battery voltage across it, so the power in each is V squared over its resistance and the total power is the sum of the two.
Step 6. Electric power in a resistor, P = V^2/R (from P = V I and Ohm's law), summed over the two parallel resistors: P = V^2 (1/R1 + 1/R2). Resistors in parallel across an ideal battery each have the whole emf across them, so each dissipates V^2/R, and the total dissipated power is the sum of these two terms. P = V**2*(1/R1 + 1/R2)  (SI units). P = (12)**2*(1/(6) + 1/(12)) = 36 (SI) = 36 W.

Step 8. Answer: total power dissipated by the resistors: 36 W.

items.description: molar gas constant, a stated constant
items.name: R

items: The gas is ideal and classical, in thermal equilibrium, and only the translational motion of the molecules counts.

steps.text: In the kinetic theory of an ideal gas the mean translational kinetic energy depends only on temperature. Find the mean kinetic energy per mole, then convert it to a speed using the molar mass: the rms speed is the speed whose kinetic energy equals this mean.

steps.description: mean translational kinetic energy of one mole of molecules
steps.principle: Equipartition theorem for translation: each molecule has mean kinetic energy (3/2) k_B T, so one mole has (3/2) R T
steps.why: The gas is ideal and classical, so the three translational degrees of freedom each carry (1/2) k_B T on average. Using the molar gas constant R gives the energy of one mole of molecules from the temperature alone.

steps.principle: Definition of the root-mean-square speed through the mean kinetic energy, (1/2) M v_rms^2 = Ek per mole
steps.why: The mean kinetic energy per mole equals half the molar mass times the mean square speed, and the rms speed is the square root of that mean square, so v_rms = sqrt(2 Ek / M); the molar mass must be in kilograms per mole.

steps.text: The result equals sqrt(3 R T / M), the standard kinetic-theory formula. Lighter molecules are faster at the same temperature, the speed grows as the square root of the absolute temperature, and typical speeds are of the order of hundreds of metres per second, comparable to the speed of sound.

Step 1. Find the root-mean-square speed of the molecules, in m/s.
Step 2. Given: T = 300 K (temperature of the gas; given); M = 4 g/mol (molar mass of the gas; given); R = 8.314 J/(mol*K) (molar gas constant, a stated constant; stated constant)
Step 3. Assumptions: The gas is ideal and classical, in thermal equilibrium, and only the translational motion of the molecules counts. The molar gas constant has the stated value.
Step 4. Approach: In the kinetic theory of an ideal gas the mean translational kinetic energy depends only on temperature. Find the mean kinetic energy per mole, then convert it to a speed using the molar mass: the rms speed is the speed whose kinetic energy equals this mean.
Step 5. Equipartition theorem for translation: each molecule has mean kinetic energy (3/2) k_B T, so one mole has (3/2) R T. The gas is ideal and classical, so the three translational degrees of freedom each carry (1/2) k_B T on average. Using the molar gas constant R gives the energy of one mole of molecules from the temperature alone. Ek = 3*R*T/2  (SI units). Ek = 3*(8.314)*(300)/2 = 3741 (SI) = 3.741 kJ/mol.
Step 6. Definition of the root-mean-square speed through the mean kinetic energy, (1/2) M v_rms^2 = Ek per mole. Step 2. Given: T = 300 K (temperature of the gas; given); M = 4 g/mol (molar mass of the gas; given); R = 8.314 J/(mol*K) (molar gas constant, a stated constant; stated constant)
Step 3. Assumptions: The gas is ideal and classical, in thermal equilibrium, and only the translational motion of the molecules counts. The molar gas constant has the stated value.
Step 4. The added sentence ("A heater warms this gas sample by 200 K and then lets it cool back before its molecular speeds are measured.") gives 200 K. This quantity has no path to the target: the sample cools back to its earlier temperature before its speeds are measured, so the measurement is at the stated temperature. It is not an input of any relation below, so it is not used and the answer is the base answer.
Step 5. Approach: In the kinetic theory of an ideal gas the mean translational kinetic energy depends only on temperature. Find the mean kinetic energy per mole, then convert it to a speed using the molar mass: the rms speed is the speed whose kinetic energy equals this mean.
Step 6. Equipartition theorem for translation: each molecule has mean kinetic energy (3/2) k_B T, so one mole has (3/2) R T. The gas is ideal and classical, so the three translational degrees of freedom each carry (1/2) k_B T on average. Using the molar gas constant R gives the energy of one mole of molecules from the temperature alone. Ek = 3*R*T/2  (SI units). Ek = 3*(8.314)*(300)/2 = 3741 (SI) = 3.741 kJ/mol.
Step 7. Definition of the root-mean-square speed through the mean kinetic energy, (1/2) M v_rms^2 = Ek per mole. The mean kinetic energy per mole equals half the molar mass times the mean square speed, and the rms speed is the square root of that mean square, so v_rms = sqrt(2 Ek / M); the molar mass must be in kilograms per mole. vrms = sqrt(2*Ek/M)  (SI units). vrms = sqrt(2*(3741)/(0.004)) = 1368 (SI) = 1368 m/s.
Step 8. Check: The result equals sqrt(3 R T / M), the standard kinetic-theory formula. Lighter molecules are faster at the same temperature, the speed grows as the square root of the absolute temperature, and typical speeds are of the order of hundreds of metres per second, comparable to the speed of sound.
Step 9. Answer: root-mean-square speed of the molecules: 1368 m/s.

items: The gas is ideal and classical, in thermal equilibrium, and only the translational motion of the molecules counts.

steps.text: The added sentence ("Before the molecular speeds are measured, a heater warms this gas sample in its flask by 100 K.") gives q = 100 K. Warming the gas sample itself by q before the speeds are measured gives it the equilibrium temperature T + q; v_rms depends only on that temperature and the molar mass. In the kinetic theory of an ideal gas the mean translational kinetic energy depends only on temperature. Find the mean kinetic energy per mole, then convert it to a speed using the molar mass: the rms speed is the speed whose kinetic energy equals this mean.

steps.description: mean translational kinetic energy of one mole of molecules
steps.principle: Equipartition theorem for translation: each molecule has mean kinetic energy (3/2) k_B T, so one mole has (3/2) R T
steps.why: The gas is ideal and classical, so the three translational degrees of freedom each carry (1/2) k_B T on average. Using the molar gas constant R gives the energy of one mole of molecules from the temperature alone.

steps.principle: Definition of the root-mean-square speed through the mean kinetic energy, (1/2) M v_rms^2 = Ek per mole
steps.why: The mean kinetic energy per mole equals half the molar mass times the mean square speed, and the rms speed is the square root of that mean square, so v_rms = sqrt(2 Ek / M); the molar mass must be in kilograms per mole.

steps.text: The result equals sqrt(3 R T / M), the standard kinetic-theory formula. Lighter molecules are faster at the same temperature, the speed grows as the square root of the absolute temperature, and typical speeds are of the order of hundreds of metres per second, comparable to the speed of sound.
root-mean-square speed of the molecules: 1579 m/s

Step 3. Assumptions: The gas is ideal and classical, in thermal equilibrium, and only the translational motion of the molecules counts. The molar gas constant has the stated value.
Step 4. The added sentence ("Before the molecular speeds are measured, a heater warms this gas sample in its flask by 100 K.") gives q = 100 K. In the graph this changes the input T (temperature of the gas): T' = T + q = 300 + 100 = 400 K. Every later step uses the changed T.
Step 5. Approach: In the kinetic theory of an ideal gas the mean translational kinetic energy depends only on temperature. Find the mean kinetic energy per mole, then convert it to a speed using the molar mass: the rms speed is the speed whose kinetic energy equals this mean.
Step 6. Equipartition theorem for translation: each molecule has mean kinetic energy (3/2) k_B T, so one mole has (3/2) R T. The gas is ideal and classical, so the three translational degrees of freedom each carry (1/2) k_B T on average. Using the molar gas constant R gives the energy of one mole of molecules from the temperature alone. Ek = 3*R*T/2  (SI units). Ek = 3*(8.314)*(400)/2 = 4988 (SI) = 4.988 kJ/mol.

Step 8. Check: The result equals sqrt(3 R T / M), the standard kinetic-theory formula. Lighter molecules are faster at the same temperature, the speed grows as the square root of the absolute temperature, and typical speeds are of the order of hundreds of metres per second, comparable to the speed of sound.
Step 9. Answer: root-mean-square speed of the molecules: 1579 m/s.

In the kinetic theory of an ideal gas the mean translational kinetic energy depends only on temperature. Find the mean kinetic energy per mole, then convert it to a speed using the molar mass: the rms speed is the speed whose kinetic energy equals this mean.

steps.description: mean translational kinetic energy of one mole of molecules
steps.principle: Equipartition theorem for translation: each molecule has mean kinetic energy (3/2) k_B T, so one mole has (3/2) R T
steps.why: The gas is ideal and classical, so the three translational degrees of freedom each carry (1/2) k_B T on average. Using the molar gas constant R gives the energy of one mole of molecules from the temperature alone.

steps.principle: Definition of the root-mean-square speed through the mean kinetic energy, (1/2) M v_rms^2 = Ek per mole
steps.why: The mean kinetic energy per mole equals half the molar mass times the mean square speed, and the rms speed is the square root of that mean square, so v_rms = sqrt(2 Ek / M); the molar mass must be in kilograms per mole.

steps.text: The result equals sqrt(3 R T / M), the standard kinetic-theory formula. Lighter molecules are faster at the same temperature, the speed grows as the square root of the absolute temperature, and typical speeds are of the order of hundreds of metres per second, comparable to the speed of sound.
root-mean-square speed of the molecules minus system B's: -412.3 m/s

Step 2. Given: T = 300 K (temperature of the gas; given); M = 4 g/mol (molar mass of the gas; given); R = 8.314 J/(mol*K) (molar gas constant, a stated constant; stated constant)
Step 3. Assumptions: The gas is ideal and classical, in thermal equilibrium, and only the translational motion of the molecules counts. The molar gas constant has the stated value.
Step 4. The added sentence ("A reference gas B has molecules with a root-mean-square speed of 1780 m/s.") gives the corresponding value for system B, 1780 m/s. The question asks for this system's answer minus system B's.
Step 5. Approach: In the kinetic theory of an ideal gas the mean translational kinetic energy depends only on temperature. Find the mean kinetic energy per mole, then convert it to a speed using the molar mass: the rms speed is the speed whose kinetic energy equals this mean.
Step 6. Equipartition theorem for translation: each molecule has mean kinetic energy (3/2) k_B T, so one mole has (3/2) R T. The gas is ideal and classical, so the three translational degrees of freedom each carry (1/2) k_B T on average. Using the molar gas constant R gives the energy of one mole of molecules from the temperature alone. Ek = 3*R*T/2  (SI units). Ek = 3*(8.314)*(300)/2 = 3741 (SI) = 3.741 kJ/mol.
Step 7. Definition of the root-mean-square speed through the mean kinetic energy, (1/2) M v_rms^2 = Ek per mole. The mean kinetic energy per mole equals half the molar mass times the mean square speed, and the rms speed is the square root of that mean square, so v_rms = sqrt(2 Ek / M); the molar mass must be in kilograms per mole. vrms = sqrt(2*Ek/M)  (SI units). vrms = sqrt(2*(3741)/(0.004)) = 1368 (SI) = 1368 m/s.
Step 8. Subtract: 1368 - 1780 = -412.3 m/s.
Step 9. Check: The result equals sqrt(3 R T / M), the standard kinetic-theory formula. Lighter molecules are faster at the same temperature, the speed grows as the square root of the absolute temperature, and typical speeds are of the order of hundreds of metres per second, comparable to the speed of sound.
Step 10. Answer: root-mean-square speed of the molecules minus system B's: -412.3 m/s.

items: The constant hc has the stated value and is used for every photon energy and wavelength.

steps.text: The added sentence ("Before the wavelength is determined, the electron gains a further 90 eV in one more accelerating gap and keeps it in the drift region.") gives q = 90 eV. The question asks for the de Broglie wavelength of an electron whose kinetic energy is known. Find the momentum (multiplied by c so that it is an energy) from the kinetic energy, then apply lambda = h / p in the form hc / (p c).

steps.description: momentum of the electron multiplied by the speed of light
steps.principle: Non-relativistic kinetic energy K = p^2 / (2 m), so p c = sqrt(2 (m c^2) K).
steps.why: The electron started from rest, so the whole energy it gained is kinetic, and K is far below the rest energy, so the classical formula holds; solving for p and multiplying by c gives a momentum in energy units that matches hc.

steps.description: de Broglie wavelength of the electron
steps.principle: de Broglie relation: a particle of momentum p has the wavelength lambda = h / p = h c / (p c).
steps.why: Matter behaves as a wave with a wavelength set by its momentum, so dividing the stated hc by p c gives the wavelength directly in length units.

steps.text: The wavelength falls as one over the square root of the kinetic energy, so more energy gives a shorter wavelength. Dimensionally, hc is energy times length and p c is an energy, so the ratio is a length. For tens to hundreds of electronvolts the result is of the order of atomic spacings, which is why electrons of this energy diffract from crystals.

steps.text: The cube is at rest, so the forces on it balance: the buoyant force of the liquid pushes up, while its weight and the string tension pull down. Find the volume of the cube, then the buoyant force and the mass of the cube, and finally solve the force balance for the tension.

steps.principle: Volume of a cube, V = a^3
steps.why: The cube is completely under the surface, so it displaces exactly its own volume of liquid. Both its weight and the buoyant force are proportional to this volume, so we need it first.

steps.principle: Archimedes' principle: the buoyant force equals the weight of the displaced liquid, Fb = rho_l g V
steps.why: The cube is fully submerged, so the displaced liquid has the volume of the cube and the density of the liquid. This is the upward force the liquid exerts on the cube; it needs the volume but not the mass.

steps.principle: Definition of density, rho = m / V, so m = rho_s V
steps.why: The weight of the cube is its mass times g, and the problem gives its density instead of its mass; the density times the volume gives the mass.

steps.principle: Newton's first law for a body in equilibrium: the net vertical force is zero, Fb = m g + T
steps.why: The cube is at rest, and the string is tied to the bottom of the tank, so it pulls the cube down along with its weight. The upward buoyant force must balance both, so the tension is the buoyant force minus the weight.

steps.text: Limiting case: if the density of the cube equalled that of the liquid, the buoyant force would equal the weight and the tension would be zero; the tension is positive only when the cube is less dense than the liquid, as it must be for a cube that needs to be held down. The result scales with the cube volume and with the density difference.
tension in the string: 3.92 N

The cube is at rest and completely under the surface, and the string is light, vertical and taut.
The liquid is incompressible and of uniform density.

steps.text: The added sentence ("The tank is then drained and refilled with a liquid whose density is 1150 kg/m³.") gives q = 1150 kg/m³. The tank's liquid is replaced and the string still holds the cube fully submerged, so the buoyant force is q g a^3 and the tension (q - rho_s) g a^3. In the graph this changes the input rho_l (density of the liquid): rho_l' = q = 1150 kg/m³ (was 1000 kg/m³). Every later step uses the changed rho_l.

The cube is at rest, so the forces on it balance: the buoyant force of the liquid pushes up, while its weight and the string tension pull down. Find the volume of the cube, then the buoyant force and the mass of the cube, and finally solve the force balance for the tension.

steps.principle: Volume of a cube, V = a^3
steps.why: The cube is completely under the surface, so it displaces exactly its own volume of liquid. Both its weight and the buoyant force are proportional to this volume, so we need it first.

steps.principle: Archimedes' principle: the buoyant force equals the weight of the displaced liquid, Fb = rho_l g V
steps.why: The cube is fully submerged, so the displaced liquid has the volume of the cube and the density of the liquid. This is the upward force the liquid exerts on the cube; it needs the volume but not the mass.

steps.principle: Definition of density, rho = m / V, so m = rho_s V
steps.why: The weight of the cube is its mass times g, and the problem gives its density instead of its mass; the density times the volume gives the mass.

steps.principle: Newton's first law for a body in equilibrium: the net vertical force is zero, Fb = m g + T
steps.why: The cube is at rest, and the string is tied to the bottom of the tank, so it pulls the cube down along with its weight. The upward buoyant force must balance both, so the tension is the buoyant force minus the weight.

steps.text: Limiting case: if the density of the cube equalled that of the liquid, the buoyant force would equal the weight and the tension would be zero; the tension is positive only when the cube is less dense than the liquid, as it must be for a cube that needs to be held down. The result scales with the cube volume and with the density difference.
tension in the string: 5.39 N
